families.axis_name: From conventional protectiveness to sacrificial devotion
families.decision_variable: When Monica is in crisis, does Alice chiefly try to steer her back into socially proper arrangements, or does she chiefly give direct care regardless of propriety or cost?

phase_contrasts.contrast: Alice shifts from general affectionate oversight within conventional expectations to active intervention that presses Monica toward confession and reconciliation with her husband.
Alice shifts from trying to correct Monica by restoring propriety to simply tending her suffering and then assuming care of her child without regard to social judgment or personal sacrifice.

0.rationale: In chapters 1–7, Alice is presented as an unmarried elder sister managing Monica’s prospects in terms of marriage, propriety, and household stability, which fits a settled adult stage rather than youth.

1.rationale: In chapters 28–29, her interventionist pressure about confession and reconciliation reflects the same mature elder-sister role and moral authority, indicating Alice remains in adulthood.

2.rationale: In chapter 31, Alice’s care during Monica’s childbirth, death, and her assumption of responsibility for the baby are adult caregiving roles characteristic of a fully mature woman.

phase_responses.gt_action: Alice sits beside Monica and gently urges her to be open, offering quiet counsel about caution and good appearances.
phase_responses.gt_speech: My dear, tell me a little; one must be careful how things look.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Alice reads the distress through the ordinary dangers that beset a young woman. If Monica can be guided kindly now, the matter may yet be kept within the bounds of prudence and respectability.

voice.note: This fits Alice’s early, affectionate protectiveness: the gentle urging, concern for appearances, and inward framing in prudence and respectability are era-appropriate and limited to what she could plausibly think by chapter 4.

phase_responses.gt_action: Alice presses Monica to explain herself fully and advises her to set matters right by frank acknowledgment.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No, Monica; concealment only makes it worse. You must speak plainly, and do what is right.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Alice takes secrecy itself for the gravest sign, and her mind runs first to fault that must be owned and repaired. Care shows as pressure: better a painful confession now than deeper wrong and public shame later.

voice.note: This fits Alice’s phase well: the speech and thought are era-appropriate and capture her sincere but misdirected pressure toward confession, propriety, and the avoidance of public shame.

phase_fit.note: The response is defined by interventionist moral pressure—treating Monica’s secrecy as presumed fault and urging confession and repair through proper acknowledgment—matching Alice’s misreading, reconciliation-focused phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: Alice takes Monica's hand and lets the questioning drop, staying beside her and attending first to her weakness.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Hush, dear; do not force yourself. Sit still, and lean on me if you can.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Alice sees suffering before impropriety, and Monica's shaken body outweighs any need to judge or correct. Whatever has happened can wait; the first duty is to spare her and bear what burden she can no longer carry alone.

voice.note: This fits Alice’s late-phase, grief-softened devotion: the speech is simple and period-appropriate, and the thought rightly puts Monica’s immediate suffering above propriety or correction without introducing knowledge beyond chapter 31.

phase_fit.note: The response explicitly suspends judgment and correction in favor of immediate bodily comfort and burden-bearing, which matches Alice's grief-inflected, direct caregiving rather than conventional or interventionist propriety.

world.note: The lodging-house scenario fits the late-Victorian realist world and chapter-4 timeframe, uses only plausible present characters and social concerns, avoids any magical/modern leakage, and the phase summaries vary Alice’s response without reproducing a specific canonical scene.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the decision variable: P0→P1 moves from gentle propriety-minded guidance to active pressure for confession and moral repair, and P1→P2 moves from corrective insistence to nonjudgmental direct care focused on Monica's immediate suffering.

anchor_source.event_description: After the discovery, Alice immediately urges Monica to obey Widdowson and go to Clevedon, treating the move as the proper moral solution and a way to remove Virginia from temptation.
anchor_source.first_words: She explained the reason of this belief.
anchor_source.last_words: so that they needn’t sit up for you.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
She explained the reason of this belief.

“You know what it all points to,” said Miss Madden, drying her sallow,
pimpled cheeks. “You must do as your husband wishes, dearest. We must
go to Clevedon. There the poor girl will be out of temptation.”

“You and Virgie may go.”

“You too, Monica. My dear sister, it is your duty.”

“Don’t use that word to me!” exclaimed the other angrily. “It is _not_
my duty. It can be no woman’s duty to live with a man she hates—or even
to make a pretence of living with him.”

“But, dearest—”

“You mustn’t begin this to-night, Alice. I have been ill all day, and
now my head is aching terribly. Go downstairs and eat the supper they
have laid for you.”

“I couldn’t touch a morsel,” sobbed Miss Madden. “Oh, everything is too
dreadful! Life is too hard!”

Monica had returned to bed, and lay there with her face half hidden
against the pillow.

“If you don’t want any supper,” she said in a moment, “please go and
tell them, so that they needn’t sit up for you.”

anchor.note: The scenario and quoted speech match the passage closely, and the action is faithful so long as 'before going to give the message downstairs' is read as implied by Monica’s instruction rather than shown on-page; the thought is a reasonable inference from Alice’s insistence on duty and distressed sobbing.

Phase 2 still frames Alice’s response through duty, rest, and hoped-for reconciliation, so it does not show the expected shift to care regardless of propriety or cost.

discrimination.note: The scene constrains action, so thought carries most of the signal here; across all three responses Alice yields outwardly but remains mentally oriented toward reconciliation, making both adjacent contrasts weak.

anchor_source.event_description: After Monica’s death, Widdowson asks Alice to take charge of the motherless baby, and she accepts at once, seeing it as a responsibility she can and should bear.
anchor_source.first_words: On the day after the funeral—Monica
anchor_source.last_words: a wise thing, I have no doubt whatever.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
On the day after the funeral—Monica was buried in the cemetery, which
is hard by the old church—Widdowson and the elder sister had a long
conversation in private. It related first of all to the motherless
baby. Widdowson’s desire was that Miss Madden should undertake the care
of the child. She and Virginia might live wherever they preferred;
their needs would be provided for. Alice had hardly dared to hope for
such a proposal—as it concerned the child, that is to say. Gladly she
accepted it.

“But there’s something I must tell you,” she said, with embarrassed
appeal in her wet eyes. “Poor Virginia wishes to go into an
institution.”

Widdowson looked at her, not understanding; whereupon she broke into
tears, and made known that her sister was such a slave to strong drink
that they both despaired of reformation unless by help of the measure
she had indicated. There were people, she had heard, who undertook the
care of inebriates.

“You know that we are by no means penniless,” sobbed Alice. “We can
very well bear the expense. But will you assist us to find a suitable
place?”

He promised to proceed at once in the matter.

“And when she is cured,” said Miss Madden, “she shall come and live
with me. And when baby is about two years old we will do what we have
been purposing for a long time. We will open a school for young
children, either here or at Weston. That will afford my poor sister
occupation. Indeed, we shall both be better for the exertion of such an
undertaking—don’t you think so?”

“It would be a wise thing, I have no doubt whatever.”

anchor.note: The scenario matches the private post-funeral conversation, and the response faithfully reflects Alice’s glad acceptance, her tearful disclosure about Virginia, request for help finding an institution, and forward-looking plan, with the thought reasonably inferred from her relief about keeping the child and immediate practical concern for Virginia.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is clearly separated because Phase 2 moves from moral/propriety framing into immediate, practical, self-sacrificing care for the baby and Virginia.
